articles.title: COP31 explained: What’s at stake at this year’s UN climate summit?
articles.summary: The world has more tools than ever to tackle climate change, yet millions remain unable to benefit from them. As clean energy technologies advance faster than ever, the challenge facing countries at COP31 is no longer just finding solutions – but making sure everyone can afford them.
articles.content:
Catastrophic floods, deadly heatwaves and prolonged droughts have been a hallmark of 2026, a year in which scientists confirmed that the world is on track to exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold.

Against this backdrop, and with a powerful El Niño expected to intensify climate impacts further, representatives of more than 190 countries will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November for COP31, the latest iteration of the keynote annual UN climate conference.

While fossil fuels remain the main driver of warming emissions, the technologies needed to move away from them are advancing at an extraordinary pace. Solar power, electric vehicles and battery storage are becoming increasingly accessible.

Yet many countries continue to struggle to benefit from them. Why?

Ahead of the summit, UN News spoke with Selwin Hart, the UN Special Adviser on Climate Action and Just Transition, about what's at stake, what’s holding back progress and what another round of climate diplomacy can realistically achieve.

What is COP31 and why does it matter?

COP stands for Conference of the Parties, in this case, the countries that are parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). These annual gatherings allow governments to assess progress and negotiate how to tackle a challenge that no nation can solve alone.

The talks produced the landmark Paris Agreement in 2015, when countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

COPs now extend well beyond government negotiations. Businesses, scientists, Indigenous Peoples, young people and civil society increasingly participate, reflecting the scale of the challenge.

“There’s now a clear recognition that addressing the climate crisis requires all hands on deck,” Mr. Hart explains.

Ministry of Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, Tuvalu Government

What can a COP actually achieve?

A COP is often judged by the agreement reached at the end, sometimes after days of difficult discussions and last-minute compromises. But Mr. Hart argues that this tells only part of the story.

He identifies three ways these conferences can make a difference:

Negotiated agreements: Countries seek consensus on issues such as climate finance, emissions reductions and adaptation, though geopolitical divisions often make ambitious outcomes difficult. The Action Agenda: Governments, development banks, businesses and civil society organizations work together on practical solutions, from expanding renewable energy and modernizing electricity networks to reducing methane emissions. National commitments: Countries use COPs to announce actions at home, including new climate plans, commitments to move away from fossil fuels and contributions to climate funds.

“There’s sometimes this expectation that COPs will always have this big grand deal that will solve the climate crisis. That’s not realistic,” Mr. Hart says.

There’s sometimes this expectation that COPs will always have this big grand deal that will solve the climate crisis. That’s not realistic

This year, Türkiye will host and preside, while Australia is leading the negotiations, working closely with Pacific Island countries.

The summit places particular emphasis on implementation, with Türkiye promoting initiatives on clean energy, food security, resilient cities, greener industries, oceans and waste reduction.

“I’m running a personal campaign to rename the Action Agenda, the Implementation Agenda,” says the top climate adviser, underscoring the need to move beyond promises and focus on practical solutions.

© Adobe Stock/Nantiya

So, what's on the table in Antalya?

Behind the diplomatic language are decisions that could affect millions of lives. Several major issues remain unresolved:

Climate finance: Developing countries want wealthier nations to fulfil their financial commitments under the Paris Agreement, while disagreements persist over funding responsibilities, access to finance and how global financial flows can be directed towards climate action. Just transition: Countries agreed last year to establish a mechanism to support the shift to cleaner economies – but still need to decide how it will work. Adaptation: Negotiators will continue to work on measuring progress while developing countries press for greater financial support. Cutting emissions: Governments remain divided over how to strengthen emissions action and deliver on existing commitments.

COP31 will also launch the second global stocktake, the Paris Agreement’s formal process for assessing collective progress towards its long-term goals.

But, haven’t we already lost the fight against global warming?

Scientists warn that the world is set to temporarily exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold, a situation known as overshoot. But how far temperatures rise, and for how long, still depends on the choices governments, businesses and societies make today.

“Overshoot is not surrender. Overshoot should really lead to a much greater degree of urgency,” Mr Hart says, calling for faster emissions cuts and greater investment in protecting vulnerable communities.

Despite the warning, he sees reasons for optimism.

“The good news in this horrible situation of overshoot is that the world has never been better equipped to solve this challenge,” he says, pointing to the rapid expansion of electric vehicles, solar energy and battery storage.

What's giving us hope? © Adobe Stock/Rh2010 Just a decade ago, the clean energy transition looked very different. The technological frontier is expanding at a remarkable pace. Electric vehicles: Ten years ago, fewer than one in 100 new cars sold worldwide was electric. In 2025, it was one in four, and that share is expected to reach 28 per cent in 2026.

Ten years ago, fewer than one in 100 new cars sold worldwide was electric. In 2025, it was one in four, and that share is expected to reach 28 per cent in 2026. Solar power: The world added more than 600 gigawatts of solar power capacity in 2025, accounting for over three-quarters of new renewable power capacity.

The world added more than 600 gigawatts of solar power capacity in 2025, accounting for over three-quarters of new renewable power capacity. Battery storage: Global battery storage capacity is now 11 times higher than in 2021. In 2025 alone, the world added 108 GW – 40 per cent more than the previous year. These systems allow electricity generated by solar panels and wind turbines to be stored and used later

If the solutions exist, what’s holding us back?

Clean energy investment has grown rapidly, but its benefits have been far from equally distributed.

Emerging and developing economies outside China, home to nearly two-thirds of the world's population, received just 18 per cent of global clean energy investment in 2025.

Africa illustrates the challenge. Despite its enormous renewable energy potential, the continent attracts only a small share of global investment, while around 600 million people still lack access to electricity.

Mr. Hart says capital investment is one of the biggest obstacles. Financing renewable energy projects in developing countries can cost several times more than in wealthier nations, even when the technology is identical.

“So, our task now, in this second decade of the Paris Agreement, is to ensure that we remove the barriers to implementation, the barriers to faster action in these economies,” he explains.

For countries already struggling with heavy debt burdens, the challenge is particularly difficult, leaving governments with limited resources to invest in healthcare, education and climate protection.

“We need solutions on finance that will not increase debt,” Mr. Hart stresses.

COP31 will not solve the climate crisis in two weeks. But it could help remove some of the barriers standing between the solutions already available and the people who need them.

For millions living with the consequences of a warming planet, that is what will matter long after the summit ends.

Follow the latest developments from COP31 through our new podcast, Talk & Action, and our special daily coverage of the conference.

articles.personality_title: COP31: Nations unite to turn clean energy advances into real climate action
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year, countries meet at a UN climate summit called COP to discuss how to fight climate change together. This year’s meeting, COP31, will happen from November 9 to 20 in Antalya, Türkiye, as the world faces more extreme weather and rising temperatures.

**What happened** – At COP31, representatives from over 190 countries will work on important issues like climate finance, cutting pollution, and helping communities adapt to changes. The summit will focus on turning promises into practical steps, with Türkiye leading efforts on clean energy, food security, and protecting oceans. The event also starts a big review of how countries are doing with their climate goals.

**Impact** – This meeting is special because it aims to remove barriers that stop many countries, especially poorer ones, from using clean energy technologies like solar power and electric cars. Even though these technologies have improved quickly, many places still can’t afford them. The summit hopes to find ways to make these tools more accessible without adding to countries’ debts.

**What's next step** – After COP31, countries will try to put new plans into action, using the agreements and ideas from the summit. The focus will be on real change, like building cleaner cities and industries and increasing investments in clean energy, especially in developing nations.

**One-sentence takeaway** – COP31 brings countries together to turn clean energy progress into real help for people worldwide, aiming to overcome financial and practical challenges in fighting climate change.
articles.personality_title_fr: COP31 : les nations unies pour transformer les progrès de l’énergie propre en actions climatiques concrètes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, les pays se réunissent lors d’un sommet climatique de l’ONU appelé COP pour discuter de la lutte contre le changement climatique. Cette année, la COP31 aura lieu du 9 au 20 novembre à Antalya, en Turquie, alors que le monde fait face à des phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes et à la hausse des températures.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À la COP31, des représentants de plus de 190 pays travailleront sur des sujets importants comme le financement climatique, la réduction de la pollution et l’aide aux communautés pour s’adapter aux changements. Le sommet mettra l’accent sur la transformation des promesses en actions concrètes, la Turquie menant des initiatives sur l’énergie propre, la sécurité alimentaire et la protection des océans. L’événement lancera aussi un grand bilan des progrès réalisés par les pays.

**Impact** – Cette réunion est spéciale car elle vise à lever les obstacles qui empêchent de nombreux pays, surtout les plus pauvres, d’utiliser les technologies d’énergie propre comme le solaire et les voitures électriques. articles.personality_title_es: COP31: Naciones unidas para convertir avances en energía limpia en acción climática real
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, los países se reúnen en una cumbre climática de la ONU llamada COP para hablar sobre cómo enfrentar juntos el cambio climático. La COP31 de este año se realizará del 9 al 20 de noviembre en Antalya, Turquía, mientras el mundo enfrenta fenómenos climáticos extremos y aumento de temperaturas.

**Qué pasó** – En la COP31, representantes de más de 190 países trabajarán en temas clave como financiamiento climático, reducción de contaminación y ayuda a comunidades para adaptarse. La cumbre se enfocará en convertir promesas en acciones prácticas, con Turquía liderando iniciativas en energía limpia, seguridad alimentaria y protección de océanos. También se iniciará una gran revisión del progreso global.

**Impacto** – Esta reunión es importante porque busca eliminar las barreras que impiden que muchos países, especialmente los más pobres, usen tecnologías limpias como la energía solar y los autos eléctricos. Aunque estas tecnologías han avanzado rápido, muchos lugares aún no pueden pagarlas. La cumbre espera encontrar maneras de hacerlas más accesibles sin aumentar la deuda.

**Próximo paso** – Después de la COP31, los países intentarán aplicar nuevos planes basados en los acuerdos e ideas de la cumbre. El enfoque será lograr cambios reales, como construir ciudades e industrias más limpias y aumentar las inversiones en energía limpia, especialmente en países en desarrollo.

**Frase clave** – La COP31 une a los países para convertir los avances en energía limpia en ayuda real para personas en todo el mundo, superando los desafíos financieros y prácticos para enfrentar el cambio climático.

articles.title: Tiktoker 'super excited' to co-host BBC nature show
articles.summary: Naturewatch, hosted by Chris Packham, Megan McCubbin and Kyle Thomas, is being made in Bristol.
articles.content:
The UK's most followed TikTok creator says he is "super excited" to be co-hosting the BBC's latest nature programme.

Naturewatch, hosted by wildlife presenters Chris Packham, Megan McCubbin and influencer Kyle Thomas, starts on Friday on BBC Two and will run all year round.

The show, which is being produced by BBC Studios' Natural History Unit, is filmed in a secret location just south of Bristol city centre, and will celebrate the best of British nature.

Thomas, who has amassed more than 33 million followers on TikTok for his videos about animals, said Naturewatch would act as a "trusted source of really brilliant factual information" as AI becomes increasingly common on social media.

He hopes his presence on the programme will attract a younger audience.

"We're going on this learning journey together," he said, adding: "I'm super, super excited. I'm learning so much already."

He explained the show would make nature accessible to everyone, with people encouraged to send videos in for the presenters to react to.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a new BBC nature show aimed at celebrating British wildlife and making nature accessible to a broad audience, including younger viewers, which promotes environmental awareness and education.
articles.personality_title: TikTok star Kyle Thomas joins BBC's new nature show to inspire young viewers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The BBC is launching a new nature show called Naturewatch. It is designed to celebrate British wildlife and bring nature closer to people across the UK.

**What happened** – Kyle Thomas, a popular TikTok creator with over 33 million followers, will co-host Naturewatch alongside well-known wildlife presenters Chris Packham and Megan McCubbin. The show starts on Friday on BBC Two and will be filmed near Bristol. It will run throughout the year.

**Impact** – Kyle Thomas hopes the show will attract younger viewers by sharing reliable and interesting facts about animals. As social media often has false information, Naturewatch aims to be a trustworthy source. The show also invites viewers to send in their own nature videos, making it interactive and easy for everyone to join in.

**What's next step** – Naturewatch will continue airing new episodes all year, encouraging more people to learn about nature and share their experiences. Kyle and the team will keep exploring wildlife and helping viewers understand the natural world better.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Popular TikTok creator Kyle Thomas joins the BBC’s Naturewatch to make learning about British wildlife fun and trustworthy for young people.
